events.text: Across the lower domains, every temple bell has begun to ring a half-tone flat, all in the same direction. The pilgrims call it the Lean. The oldest hymn-keepers say it points to the Temple That Remembers Its Hymn, a shrine whose god died but whose closing prayer was never finished, and still has not stopped.

choices.text: Ask a hymn-keeper what the hymn is

effects.log: She hums four notes and stops, pale. The bell on the wall answers, a half-tone flat, from nowhere.

choices.text: Listen to the lean of the bells

effects.log: You stand in the courtyard until dusk. By then you can tell exactly which way the world is tilting.

events.text: {sr_sect} walks its delegation to the temple steps in procession, incense in hand, because nothing else is permitted at a shrine that is still mid-service. The leader reminds you to match the chant when it comes. The doors are open. Somewhere inside, a voice is singing the same line it has sung for six hundred years.

choices.text: Chant along from the first line

effects.log: It is not a hymn you know. But it fits your mouth like a worn glove, and the steps accept you.

choices.text: Hold the incense and stay silent

effects.log: Silence is also a kind of prayer. The doors seem to accept it, though less warmly.

events.text: You do not walk up the steps. You go round the back, to the bell-cote, where the rope hangs slack and frayed. A small door is behind it, the sort a sacristan once used to slip in late. The hymn is louder here, bright and thin, and it goes on and on, a candle-flame of sound in the dark.

choices.text: Wait for a breath in the hymn

effects.log: There is one, every ninety lines, a tiny gap like a stitch. You slip in through it unnoticed.

choices.text: Hum quietly beneath it

effects.log: You blend in as one voice among many, a candle among candles. It feels like cheating, and a little like worship.

events.text: The safe road follows the Procession Aisle, lined with votive stalls whose lamps were lit by hands long gone. Rival delegations pass each other in the half-light, sharing candles in quiet politeness. A young acolyte of another pantheon offers you a flame and asks you to remember her name. You do.

choices.text: Light your candle from hers

effects.log: It takes at once, clean and golden. She smiles, a small shy thing, and you walk on a little warmer.

choices.text: Hold your own flame close and nod

effects.log: You do not need the gift. But you do not refuse it, and she sees that.

events.text: The beast road passes through the Choir Loft, where the temple's sparrows nest among the pipes. They are not natural birds; they sing in four voices at once, and flock together in a harmony that makes the dust rise. One lands on your shoulder, chirps a single chord, and waits with wide, bright eyes.

choices.text: Hum the note back

effects.log: The sparrow tilts its head, delighted. The whole flock joins in and lifts you, nearly, off your feet.

choices.text: Brush it gently away

effects.log: It flutters up and scolds, in thirds. The loft hums with outrage for some time.

events.text: The hidden road is a spiral stair in the bell-tower, which you know by the tune of its creaking. A past life of yours rang these bells. At the top the old bell-rope is coiled round a peg, with a name stitched into the loop in thread you chose yourself. Beside it, on the bench, is the hymn's missing last line, written out in your hand.

choices.text: Read the last line aloud

effects.log: The tower trembles with relief. Far below, a voice stops mid-note, drawing breath.

choices.text: Fold the line away unsaid

effects.log: Some endings are better withheld. You keep it against your heart like a pressed flower.

events.text: The last priest lowers his hands, and the long hymn stops. He is only a shape of old cloth and candlelight, but for the first time in six hundred years he looks like a man at the end of a long day. He holds out the hymn's final verse as he would a child, and asks you, simply, to finish it for him.

choices.text: Sing the last verse

effects.log: It is short. When it ends, the whole temple exhales. The priest smiles, and the lamps go out one by one.

choices.text: Take the verse and let him rest

effects.log: The priest bows and fades like incense. The verse is warm in your hand, a living thing.

events.text: The priest does not strike. He sings, one note, and it takes the strength out of your knees. You sink onto the cold stone as the hymn rises around you, and for an hour you are one voice among a thousand, dissolved in a prayer that is not yours. When it releases you, you are somewhere near the door.

choices.text: Rest where you fell

effects.log: The stone is cool. The hymn goes on above you. It is neither kind nor unkind, only vast.

choices.text: Crawl out and look back

effects.log: The priest's eyes are closed. He is singing for something you cannot see.

events.text: You slip past the priest as he reaches for a high note, in the swell that covers all footsteps. The aisle is long and lamp-lit. You cross it in the rhythm of the hymn, step for step, and arrive at the reliquary on the final beat, breathless and quite sure you were never seen.

choices.text: Bow to the reliquary

effects.log: The little lamp flares once, in thanks. It may have been the draught.

choices.text: Count the bars you crossed

effects.log: Ninety-three. You will know the rhythm in your sleep.

events.text: {sr_sect} places the recovered verse on the high altar of its own temple and invites every priest of the delegation to sing it in turn. It takes a day. When it is done, the verse is in the mouths of everyone, and the original is a blank page. This, the leader says, is what a verse is for.

choices.text: Sing your turn at dusk

effects.log: Your voice is the thinnest of all. The verse takes it kindly, and holds the note a breath longer than you do.

choices.text: Listen from the back

effects.log: The verse passes along the hall like a cup. When it reaches you, you find you know it already.

events.text: At the temple gate, a delegation of a rival pantheon waits in white, hands folded, smiling. They say the hymn belonged to a god of theirs, once, and would be returned. They are very polite about it. They are also a great many, and the gate is narrow.

choices.text: Speak the verse aloud once, so it is no one's alone

effects.log: They listen. Nobody can own what has been sung to a crowd. They bow, stiffly, and part.

choices.text: Slip out by the sacristan's door

effects.log: It leads to the almonry. You walk out past the sleeping alms-bowls with the verse in your sleeve.

events.text: Granaries in three domains are quietly short. Offerings left at altars go missing in the night, before any god has claimed them. A worried steward of the Harvest Ministry traces it to a hall nobody has visited in nine hundred years: the Hall of Unclaimed Offerings, where everything that was ever left for a god and not taken is kept, and has begun to hunger.

choices.text: Ask the steward what is missing

effects.log: Rice, tea, cut flowers, lamp-oil, and a child's toy horse. The list ends with the horse, and she cannot say why.

choices.text: Leave an offering on your own altar and watch it

effects.log: Nothing happens until the moon sets. Then your bowl is empty, and the incense smoke runs the wrong way.

events.text: {sr_sect} enters in the dress of offering-bearers, each member carrying a tray of fresh gifts to feed the Hall's hunger before it feeds on the party. The leader instructs the party to set the trays down one by one and not look back. The hall is vast and dim, and smells of old rice and sweet smoke.

choices.text: Set your tray down gently

effects.log: The offerings vanish as you turn, with a soft sound like a sigh of relief. The hall seems calmer by a shade.

choices.text: Keep a handful in your sleeve

effects.log: It might be wise. It might be an insult. A distant sound like a hungry stomach follows you inward.

events.text: You come in through the almonry hatch, among the sacks of rice nobody ever fetched. They are stacked to the ceiling and each one is tagged with a name, a god, a date, a wish. The labels are in a thousand hands. It is the most heartbreaking filing system you have ever seen.

choices.text: Read the labels as you climb

effects.log: A harvest, a husband, a cure, a baby. The stack is high, and so is your throat. You do not stop.

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the ladder

effects.log: Some things are not for reading. You climb on, hand over hand, in grave silence.

events.text: The safe road follows the Long Altar, a table that runs the length of the hall, laid with every offering a god ever failed to take. Rival delegations walk beside it, hushed, careful not to touch. A priest of another pantheon stops to straighten a bowl of rice. Then another does the same. It spreads, bowl by bowl, down the hall.

choices.text: Straighten a bowl yourself

effects.log: The rice is cold and perfect. You straighten it, and another, and it feels like the only decent thing to do.

choices.text: Walk on quickly

effects.log: The Hall does not mind. But you feel the shape of the neglect in your shoulders, a stoop that lingers for an hour.

events.text: The beast road passes through the Pantry of Strays, where the hungry things nest: hollow-eyed temple cats, skinny and many, long-whiskered and watchful. They have been waiting centuries for a god to remember the saucer. A great ragged tom steps onto the aisle, looks at your hands, and sits down in front of you.

choices.text: Hand over the offering you carry

effects.log: The tom eats it with great and terrible dignity. The others follow in a murmuring wave.

choices.text: Step around the tom

effects.log: He lets you pass. But a hundred small eyes watch you go, and the silence is not kind.

events.text: The hidden road runs through the Pantry's back wall, behind a shelf you stocked yourself in a past life. A brass tag on the shelf reads, in your hand: for whoever remembers. On it sits a small bowl of rice that is neither stale nor cold, and a pair of chopsticks laid neatly beside it, waiting.

choices.text: Eat the rice

effects.log: It is the warmest, plainest meal of your life. When the bowl is empty, something in the Hall breathes out.

choices.text: Leave the bowl untouched and bow

effects.log: Not everything is for you. The Hall approves, in its quiet way, and the shelf shuts after you with a click.

events.text: The hunger of the Hall draws itself up into a great hollow shape of steam and ash, and then, when it sees you hold your ground without fear, it falters. It was never anger; it was longing. It sets down a single golden bowl in front of you, the prayer answered nine centuries late, and asks, in its thin way, whether it is too late to be thanked.

choices.text: Thank it, with all the words you have

effects.log: It shudders, and thins, and the golden bowl is warm. You are not sure whether it was more relieved than you.

choices.text: Take the bowl and the blessing

effects.log: It is the answer to a wish that was never yours. But it fits you now, and you carry it gently.

events.text: The hunger takes you in. It does not bite; it simply reaches, and for a moment it eats your sense of being wanted at all. You come back to yourself on the cold floor with a feeling like an empty plate. It passes. It does not pass quickly. The hall, appeased, lets you crawl out.

choices.text: Eat something from your pack at once

effects.log: Dry bread. It is the best thing you have ever tasted, and you eat every crumb.

choices.text: Lie there and think of someone

effects.log: It helps. You lie on the cold floor thinking of someone who wanted you, and the hollow slowly fills.

events.text: You slip past the hunger by setting a decoy: a plate of your own lunch, left at an empty altar, an act of small and shameless diplomacy. The hunger turns to it with a rasp of delight. You edge along the wall and out through the pantry, with your stomach rumbling in sympathy.

choices.text: Leave a second plate at the next altar

effects.log: The hunger cannot decide. It is torn between them, and you are long gone before it chooses.

choices.text: Feel a little ashamed

effects.log: It was a plain lunch. But you think of it for a week, and leave a bowl of rice on your own altar from then on.

events.text: {sr_sect} lays the prayer-answered-late on its high altar and invites every member of the delegation to say what they would have wished for, had they been among the ones the Hall remembers. It takes all night. In the morning the altar is bare, and the Hall of Unclaimed Offerings is a little less empty.

choices.text: Say your wish aloud

effects.log: It is smaller than you thought. Saying it makes it lighter, and the room seems to lean in to hear it.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself

effects.log: Some wishes are too tender for an altar. You hold it, and the night is long and kind.

events.text: Outside the Hall, a hungry pair of temple-thieves lean on the almonry wall, with the studied idleness of men who are not at all sure what they came for. They have heard the answered prayer is worth a fortune, and they are probably right. Their bag is empty and their eyes are not.

choices.text: Share a handful of what you carry

effects.log: It is not much. But their faces change, and they step aside, ashamed of the plan they never carried out.

choices.text: Walk past with a firm nod

effects.log: They are not killers. They are hungry, and they were not hungry enough, this time.

events.text: The stags of the lower plains have begun to move in a single great herd, all heading one way across a dozen domains, their antlers bound with ribbons no hunter tied. Hunters' gods lower their bows and stand aside. They say the Grove of the Antlered God is opening: a sacred wood whose god was hunted down by its own worshippers, and has never forgiven the fashion.

choices.text: Follow the herd to the plains' edge

effects.log: They flow past you in silence, hundreds of them, ribboned and breathing. The ground trembles in a slow pulse.

choices.text: Ask a hunter-god why he stands aside

effects.log: He says only that some herds are not for hunting. Then he sets down his bow, quite deliberately, and walks away.

events.text: {sr_sect} enters the Grove with all weapons slung and reversed, as the old custom demands, and a bundle of green boughs held before the chest. The leader whispers that stags see intent before they see anything else. The first trees are very tall, and between them, at the edge of sight, something large lowers its head.

choices.text: Reverse your weapon and bow

effects.log: The hush deepens. The large shape lifts its head again. You pass, slowly, between the trunks, unseen.

choices.text: Hold the boughs and think of nothing

effects.log: It is a skill like balancing a bowl. The Grove accepts the effort, if not the thought.

events.text: You enter the Grove by the poachers' path, which every stag has marked with a warning of scent. You wear a robe of cut ferns and smear your face with moss-water. Overhead the leaves close like a green hand, and the trail goes soft under your feet. A wet sniff, close by, tells you that you were not as invisible as you hoped.

choices.text: Freeze, and let the sniffing pass

effects.log: A great damp nose passes close by your ear and withdraws. You breathe again in time with the wood.

choices.text: Roll under a fallen log

effects.log: You roll, scratch your elbow, and lie with your heart in your throat. The stag steps over you, daintily.

events.text: The safe road follows the Pilgrim's Ride, a gravelled lane through the trees where rival delegations pass in single file under hanging antlers shed over ten thousand years. Each has a name carved in it, in a script nobody reads any more. You step carefully around a pile, and touch one name as you go.

choices.text: Touch a shed antler in greeting

effects.log: It is warm, and not from the sun. The name under your fingers is briefly almost legible.

choices.text: Walk with the delegation, quiet and close

effects.log: The Ride is safe for those who do not stray. You feel the herd watching, and being watched, and being quiet.

events.text: The beast road passes through the Rut-Meadow, where the great stags stand at dusk in a ring of steaming breath. They are the Grove's real law. One steps forward, antlers like a winter tree, and bows its head to the ground in front of you. It is a challenge, or a greeting. In the Grove, they are the same.

choices.text: Bow back, as low as it did

effects.log: The stag lifts its head slowly. The ring opens, without a sound, to let you through.

choices.text: Lower your hands and keep walking

effects.log: The stag does not move. But its breath follows you across the meadow, slow and warm and exact.

events.text: The hidden road is a deer-track you cut yourself, in a life when you were the herd's keeper. You know where every root is. At the end of it, in a hollow of ferns, is a crown of living antler on a stump, so old that moss has made a bed of it. The antler is still growing.

choices.text: Lift the crown

effects.log: It is lighter than it looks, alive in your hands, a warm pulse running through the tines. The stump sighs as if relieved.

choices.text: Let the crown sleep and take a single shed tine

effects.log: The crown goes on growing. Your tine is warm in your pocket, a seed of the wood.

events.text: The herd-spirit of the Antlered God rises out of the ferns in the shape of a stag made of mist and moonlight, and bows, one front leg folded, as its god once bowed to his priests. It was not a trial but a test of what you would do when you thought you had won. It steps aside, and the crown lies waiting.

choices.text: Bow in return and take the crown

effects.log: It lies against your hands like a living thing grateful to be held. The herd-spirit fades into mist.

choices.text: Ask the herd-spirit its god's name

effects.log: It lowers its head to your ear. The name is a breath of wind in leaves. You carry it away with you, unspoken.

events.text: The herd-spirit charges, not to wound but to carry. It scoops you up on its antlers and bears you through the Grove at a gallop, between trees that part like curtains, and sets you down at the border without a scratch. It watches you from the treeline, ears forward. The matter is closed.

choices.text: Laugh, breathless, at the border

effects.log: You have been escorted off a sacred wood by a ghost with antlers. It is humbling, and a good story.

choices.text: Look back at the treeline

effects.log: The herd-spirit has already turned away. It gives no second look. Some refusals are the highest courtesy.

events.text: You kneel in the ferns and put down everything you carry that could be a weapon, and then sit, hands open, until the moon is over the clearing. The herd-spirit comes close at last and breathes on your face, and it smells of rain and green and a faint sweet smoke of old offerings. It does not want to be led. It wants to be asked.

choices.text: Ask it to walk with you a while

effects.log: It does, silently, to the edge of the Grove and no further. At the border it lowers its head, and the crown is yours.

choices.text: Ask it what it grieves

effects.log: It shows you, in a flicker of mist, a hunting horn and a feast in a hall of the pantheon above. You say nothing. You kneel again.

events.text: {sr_sect} places the crown of living antler in a bed of moss on the temple altar, where it will go on growing as long as someone tends it. A rota of gardeners is drawn up. Yours is the dawn watch. The leader hands you a small silver pruning-knife and warns you against ever using it.

choices.text: Accept the dawn watch

effects.log: It is cold and hushed, and the crown grows a finger-width while you sit. You do not tell anyone how much you like it.

choices.text: Ask to carry the crown out to the Grove at the next opening

effects.log: The leader hesitates, then writes your name in the margin of the rota. It is a promise as much as a duty.

events.text: At the Grove's last ride a party of horn-sounding huntsmen has pitched a camp. They wear the green of a rival pantheon and speak politely of tradition. Their dogs, however, are not polite; they are hungry, white and silent, and they have already smelled the crown in your pack.

choices.text: Speak to the hounds in the herd-spirit's tongue

effects.log: It is the one thing you picked up. The hounds lie down, bewildered, and the huntsmen, flustered, let you pass.

choices.text: Go round through the shallows of the stream

effects.log: Water takes the scent. The hounds quarter the bank in a frustrated ring. You are long gone.

events.text: Three clerks of the Ministry of Fates have independently reported the same discrepancy: a column of fates that adds to one more than it should. A stray fate is loose in the pantheon's accounts. The auditors mutter that the Counting-House of Small Fates, long sealed, has reopened to correct it, and will be correcting anyone who gets in the way.

choices.text: Ask a clerk to show you the column

effects.log: He does, trembling. The extra fate is a minor one: a boy who was meant to sell fish, and sells lanterns instead.

choices.text: Check your own fate for errors

effects.log: You find a slip in the spelling of your birth-year. It makes you laugh aloud, and then worry.

events.text: {sr_sect} files the delegation into the Counting-House at the stroke of the hour, in order of rank, as a civil service should, each member with a ledger in hand and a stylus behind the ear. The leader insists that nobody, under any circumstances, is to correct anyone else's sums. The ledgers rustle, eager to be wrong.

choices.text: Check your arithmetic twice

effects.log: It is correct. A small clerk in the corner of the hall gives a small, approving nod.

choices.text: Add something deliberately wrong

effects.log: A bell rings softly somewhere. A clerk appears at your elbow, cross, with a red brush.

events.text: You come in through the filing-chute, where the House posts its discarded fates for burning, and land in a heap of crumpled slips. Each one is somebody's small life, a handful of lines in a neat clerk's hand. You smooth one flat, without meaning to. It describes a baker's apprenticeship that never took place.

choices.text: Put the slip back where it was

effects.log: The chute swallows it gently. Somewhere above, a bell rings once, as if satisfied.

choices.text: Keep it, and read the rest

effects.log: You learn more about the fates of strangers than you wished. It leaves you with a quiet, unwelcome tenderness.

events.text: The safe road follows the Long Counter, a mile of polished wood with a brass bell at every window. Rival delegations queue patiently, clutching their forms. The queue moves one step an hour. A tired clerk behind the nearest window offers to stamp your papers, with a wink, if you promise not to read what the stamp says.

choices.text: Promise, and take the stamp

effects.log: The stamp is green, warm and smells of plums. It opens doors you do not see until you reach them.

choices.text: Read the stamp anyway

effects.log: It says: approved with reservations. The clerk sighs. You pass, but the reservations follow.

events.text: The beast road passes the Rat Archive, a warren of paper tunnels gnawed through the old fate-bundles by clerk-mice no larger than a thumb. Each wears a tiny pince-nez of wire. A hundred of them look up as you pass, and the whisper of nibbling stops. One steps forward with a tiny scroll, and clears its throat.

choices.text: Read the scroll aloud

effects.log: It is a petition, in a very small hand, for a larger lunch break. You sign it, with a smile.

choices.text: Step carefully over the tunnels

effects.log: They watch you cross in silence. Several bow, minutely, when you are almost through.

events.text: The hidden road is a door behind the Complaints Desk that has your name on it in brass, polished by years of other people's hands. Behind it is a small office with a tidy table and a single sealed folder, your own. It contains the first draft of your fate, before the revisions, and a note: you may keep one line.

choices.text: Keep the line about courage

effects.log: It slides into your head like a key. The folder shuts, and the office goes quiet, satisfied.

choices.text: Keep the line about kindness

effects.log: It is a smaller line than you expected. It fits perfectly.

events.text: The clerk-god lays down his red brush, and for the first time his face shows a flicker of something that is not routine. You have solved his discrepancy, the stray fate, without shuffling a page. He stamps the exit form with trembling dignity, and slides across the stamped page of the Book, the one he has guarded since the House was sealed.

choices.text: Receive the page with both hands

effects.log: It is thin as a petal and heavy as a verdict. The clerk exhales for the first time in centuries.

choices.text: Ask what he would have written, if allowed

effects.log: He considers it for a long time. Then he writes a single line on his blotter, and shows it to you, and wipes it away.

events.text: The clerk-god examines your papers, tuts, and finds a fault on every page. He sends you to the back of the queue, then to the back of the other queue, then to a small room where you wait for a very long time. When at last you are called, your papers are fine, and the day is gone. This, he says, is mercy.

choices.text: Thank him for the lesson

effects.log: He nods stiffly. It may have been a joke. It may not.

choices.text: Sit and wait out the last of the queue

effects.log: There is an art to waiting. You discover, unhappily, that you are good at it.

events.text: You slip past the clerk-god by joining a line of queueing petitioners and shuffling forward in it, step by dull step, until the line reaches the exit window without any of you being asked a single question. It is the dullest, most effective escape imaginable. Your feet ache. You are, officially, a petitioner.

choices.text: Collect your stamped receipt

effects.log: It says: noted. You keep it in your sleeve as a little reminder of the gentlest bureaucracy in the heavens.

choices.text: Drop out of the queue at the door

effects.log: Nobody stops you. In a queue, everyone is anonymous. That is the whole point.

events.text: {sr_sect} files the stamped page with the pantheon's own archive, under seven seals, and a registrar reads out the receipt for the delegation. It lists each name, in order, with the fate-line each of you was permitted to keep. Yours is read out last. It is shorter than you expected, and it suits you.

choices.text: Ask the registrar to read it again

effects.log: She does, more slowly. You listen to it as you would a strange, accurate song.

choices.text: Thank the registrar and go

effects.log: She says only: noted. It is the highest thanks the archive can offer.

events.text: At the House's final turnstile, three auditors in grey wait with a ledger and a very short pencil. They would like to know why the Counting-House records one fewer small fate than it did this morning. They are in no hurry. They have a chair for you, and a cup of tea, and a form.

choices.text: Fill in the form honestly

effects.log: It takes an hour. The auditors, to their credit, are fair. They stamp it and let you go, a little lighter in conscience.

choices.text: Ask for a second form to fill in first

effects.log: It is a gambit as old as the House. By the time they find it, you are outside, whistling.

events.text: Gulls the colour of ash have appeared over the temple harbours, crying a single, unmistakable word: please. Ship-gods mark the tide-tables with a worried hand. Beneath the Sea of Faith, they say, the Shore of Spent Prayers is rising: the beach where every prayer that went unanswered washes up, and where a ferryman waits for those who come to claim them.

choices.text: Walk the harbour at low tide

effects.log: The mud is full of tiny shells, each with a word inside. You pick one up. It says: tomorrow.

choices.text: Ask a ship-god what the gulls say

effects.log: He replies in a very small voice that they say what everyone says in the end. Then he goes to mend a net.

events.text: {sr_sect} brings its delegation to the shingle in a long barge with a black prow, painted by the Ministry of Funerals, and the ferryman's lamp comes bobbing across the dark water to meet it. The leader holds a coin of silver on the tongue as the custom demands. The shore ahead is pale and endless, and whispers.

choices.text: Hold the coin and say nothing

effects.log: The lamp tilts toward you, then away. A silent passage is the most respected kind.

choices.text: Whisper your own prayer to the water

effects.log: It is taken, carefully, as one takes a letter. You feel suddenly very light.

events.text: You walk out along the breakwater at the lowest tide of the year, where the sea has drawn back from the shingle and left a path for one night. It is lined with tiny bottles, each corked and sealed in wax, each holding a word. The wind blows through them and they sing, like a flute in a thousand parts.

choices.text: Walk quickly along the breakwater

effects.log: The song follows you, rising and falling. You reach the shore with the tune in your head for days.

choices.text: Stop and listen to one bottle

effects.log: It says a name. You do not know it. You say it back, and the bottle goes quiet, at peace.

events.text: The safe road is the Strand, a broad pale beach where rival delegations pace in the shallows, collecting the shells they were sent for. Each shell is a prayer. Many are the same prayer. The sand shifts and whispers underfoot, and every footprint fills with small cold water.

choices.text: Pick up one shell for each of your party

effects.log: It takes an hour. Each one you read quietly, and none of them are easy.

choices.text: Collect shells for someone you left behind

effects.log: You do, and it is a heavy basket. But it is the right kind of heavy.

events.text: The beast road passes the Tide-Pools, where creatures grown from the beach's loneliness crawl and drift: pale crabs with the faces of old men, anemones that hum, a long grey eel with a woman's gentle eyes. They gather to look at your lamp. None of them, you realise, has been looked at in a very long time.

choices.text: Hold the lamp lower so they can see you

effects.log: They come to the edge of the pool and sit. You stay with them a while. It is very quiet, and no one hurries you.

choices.text: Walk on, carrying the light high

effects.log: They follow the glow to the edge of the Tide-Pools, longingly. You feel their eyes on your back for a mile.

events.text: The hidden road is a path of black stepping-stones across the shallows, laid by a hand you remember better than your own. At the end is a driftwood hut, and in the hut a small shelf of prayers of yours, spent in lives gone by. They are all small, and all sincere. One of them, you realise, was answered after all.

choices.text: Find the answered one

effects.log: It is the smallest of the lot. You hold it, a long time, and it grows warm and then quiet.

choices.text: Take the lot and carry it out to sea

effects.log: You wade into the sea and let them go, one at a time. The water takes them kindly, and does not give them back.

events.text: The ferryman lowers his oar. He has rowed the unanswered across for so long that he has lost the sense of what he was rowing them toward. When you stand firm and answer his question straight, he turns his lantern over and pours its light out onto the shingle. It gathers into a single lamp, lit with one answered prayer, and he presses it into your hand.

choices.text: Take the lamp with thanks

effects.log: It is warm. For the first time in his long life, the ferryman smiles, and puts up his oar.

choices.text: Ask him what he would have prayed for

effects.log: He tells you. It is small and sweet and entirely achievable. You carry it back to the world as a debt.

events.text: The ferryman rows you out past the breakers and back again, three times, without speaking. When the barge finally touches the shingle he has said one sentence, and it was a kindness. You are too tired to remember it. It will come back, over the years, at odd moments, like a small warm stone in the pocket.

choices.text: Thank him for the crossing

effects.log: He nods and pushes off again into the fog. The sound of his oar goes on a long time.

choices.text: Lie on the shingle and rest

effects.log: The shells whisper at your ear in a hundred voices. After a while, you learn to tell them apart.

events.text: You slip past the ferryman by laying your coin on the shingle and walking away from it, quite deliberately, and in the opposite direction. He stares after you across the water. It is a trick as old as the Shore: the ferryman is bound to the coin, not the traveller. You are on the strand, free, and slightly haunted.

choices.text: Leave the coin as a gift

effects.log: He picks it up. It is the first fare in decades that did not require him to take anyone anywhere.

choices.text: Look back from the dunes

effects.log: He is standing in the shallows, holding the coin up to the light. He looks, you decide, quite pleased.

events.text: {sr_sect} sets the lantern lit with one answered prayer on the harbour wall of its principal temple, and keeps it burning there by turns. It becomes a place of pilgrimage within the month. A queue forms. At night the lamp is lowered and the leader reads out the most recent prayers, and no one asks which one was answered.

choices.text: Take a turn at the lamp

effects.log: Your watch is the second night. The lamp is a small steady thing, and it asks nothing of you but that you stay.

choices.text: Add a prayer of your own to the line

effects.log: You write it, and fold it, and put it in the basket. It is the first prayer you have said in years.

events.text: On the quay a pair of salvage-priests in grey stand by a cart with a brass-bound chest, offering to buy the answered lamp on behalf of the poor. They have a letter of authority, and a very kind manner, and a way of not blinking. Behind them, in the lee of the warehouse, another cart waits with a net.

choices.text: Ask to see where the poor are

effects.log: They hesitate. The question is an honest one. They lead you, resentfully, to the harbour almshouse, and the lamp is not mentioned again.

choices.text: Disappear into the tide-market crowd

effects.log: Stalls of fish, shell and rope. You are one more bargain-hunter with a lantern and a shawl.

events.text: Gods across the middle heavens have begun to sleep late and wake puzzled, with other people's memories in their mouths. The Oracle of the Second Hour traces the leak to a domain that sank beneath its own god's dream, long ago, and has come up for air. The god is still asleep inside it. Everything in the domain is something he is dreaming.

choices.text: Ask the Oracle whose dream it is

effects.log: She says his name and then forgets she has said it. The room goes cold, and she asks you to leave, kindly.

choices.text: Write down what you dreamed last night

effects.log: It is a corridor you do not know, with a door you almost opened. You keep the page against need.

events.text: {sr_sect} wades into the dream-domain in a loose line, hands joined, because the old rule says no one should sleepwalk alone. The leader counts heads every hundred steps. The sky ahead is a soft grey-gold that does not quite match the ground. A bell rings somewhere that is not exactly a place.

choices.text: Hold the hands on either side tightly

effects.log: Their palms are warm and real. It is the one thing in the domain that is.

choices.text: Count your own steps instead

effects.log: A thousand, then two, then an odd number. The domain loses its patience with you, slightly, and lets you through.

events.text: You enter by lying down on the step of the abandoned shrine at the domain's edge and falling asleep, as the old stories advise. When you open your eyes you are standing in a long white hall full of doors, each marked with a different god's face. A smell of warm bread and old rain drifts from the farthest.

choices.text: Try the door with the sleeper's face

effects.log: It opens on a bedroom you half-know. Someone sleeping in it turns over and murmurs a name.

choices.text: Walk straight down the hall without looking

effects.log: It takes longer than it should. But at the end the doors fold away, and you step through into the dream proper.

events.text: The safe road follows the Lane of Memory, a street that remembers being a street. Rival delegations walk it in tidy rows, passing shopfronts that dissolve when looked at too long. Each turns away from its own reflection. A baker sets out a tray of bread that smells of home and has no crust. You do not eat it.

choices.text: Walk on, eyes on the horizon

effects.log: The shops are a murmur at the edge of sight. The lane thins to a mere path, and then a plank bridge.

choices.text: Ask the baker whose bread it is

effects.log: He looks surprised to be asked. Then he says it is the god's mother's, and goes back to kneading. A tear lands in the dough.

events.text: The beast road runs through the Menagerie of Nightmares, a wide meadow full of the god's fears given a gentle, ridiculous shape: a hippopotamus in a tie, a very anxious owl, a tall moth with a lawyer's eyes. They stand about like guests at a bad party. One steps forward, hat in hand, and clears its throat.

choices.text: Hear the creature out

effects.log: It is afraid of being forgotten. You promise, rashly, that you will not. The meadow lets out a long, grateful breath.

choices.text: Back away slowly

effects.log: They watch you go with sad, mild faces. One waves. You are, perhaps, a little unkind.

events.text: The hidden road is an alley that was never on the dreamer's map, a place he did not know he knew. You walk it with a light, certain step. At the end is a small garden gate, and beyond it a bench, and on the bench a folded note in your handwriting: wake him gently. Underneath, a dream the god never finished.

choices.text: Take the unfinished dream

effects.log: It is warm and humming, a roll of silk that fits in the palm. Beyond the gate, someone sighs in their sleep.

choices.text: Sit on the bench a while

effects.log: The garden hums. When you rise, you have been somewhere, and cannot say where, and are the better for it.

events.text: The dreaming god's waking self stirs, a tall, gentle figure with eyes closed, and for a long moment the whole domain holds its breath. It knows it is being dreamed. It knows, now, that you are not. It lifts a hand, and in that hand is the unfinished dream, offered like a child to a stranger it has decided to trust.

choices.text: Take the dream and bow

effects.log: It is the lightest weight you have ever carried. The god sighs, and the sky above you lightens by a shade.

choices.text: Promise to wake him gently

effects.log: He smiles, asleep. You will have to keep the promise, and you will.

events.text: The waking self opens its eyes, once, and looks at you. In that look is every dream the god ever had of a stranger, and for a long, bright moment you are all of them. When it closes its eyes you are lying in the grey-gold grass, hearing your own heartbeat as though it were a drum in another room.

choices.text: Lie still until your breath is your own

effects.log: It takes a long time. But you rise, at last, as yourself, a little forgiven and a little dazed.

choices.text: Try to remember what you saw

effects.log: A door, a garden, a name. You hold onto the name until it dissolves.

events.text: You slip past the waking self by becoming, for a moment, a part of the dream: you adopt the dull drift of a figure in a crowd, a dreamer's extra. The waking self looks directly at you, finds you wholly unremarkable, and looks away. It is an insult you accept with gratitude.

choices.text: Keep drifting until the border

effects.log: The extras drift in a slow tide toward the edge of the dream. You flow with them and are carried, unremarked, out.

choices.text: Stop and bow to the sleeper

effects.log: He does not wake. But a small smile flickers on a face of cloud, and you walk on easier.

events.text: {sr_sect} sets the unfinished dream on the high altar of the Ministry of Sleep, under a veil of black silk, and sends for the god's kin to witness. They come, one by one, and each says a name softly and goes away. The dream hums, stirs, and for one night the whole temple sleeps well.

choices.text: Stay awake to keep the vigil

effects.log: It is the strangest night of your life. At dawn, the dream is a little further finished, and you do not know how.

choices.text: Sleep in the temple with the others

effects.log: You dream of a bakery with no crust. You wake with the taste of warm bread, and a quiet heart.

events.text: At the domain's edge a tall woman in the grey of the Ministry of Sleep stands with her hands folded in her sleeves. She asks, kindly, for the dream, which has been entrusted to her Ministry for all the ages. The folds of her sleeves hold something heavy, and the watchful guards behind her are yawning in perfectly unison.

choices.text: Yawn back, and slip out while they sleep

effects.log: The yawn is catching. Half the guards drop where they stand. You walk through the slumbering line, breath held, grinning.

choices.text: Ask her to wait until the god wakes to decide

effects.log: She considers it. It is a fair request, and she is a fair woman. She steps aside, gravely.

events.text: A hairline crack has opened in the vault of the old heavens, and through it, every night, comes a sound like a very large door settling on its hinges. The Ministry of Rites confirms what the scholars feared: the Sealed Heaven of the Dead Pantheon is opening. Twelve thrones, twelve laws, and not one god left to excuse a breach of them.

choices.text: Ask the scholars which laws

effects.log: They list eleven. The twelfth, they say, was never recorded, because those who learned it did not return to say.

choices.text: Read the Rites for guests

effects.log: There is a clause about carrying fire, and another about leaving no debt unpaid. You copy both, in a careful hand.

events.text: {sr_sect} approaches the Sealed Heaven with a banner of mourning, since entering a dead pantheon's house is, by the oldest of laws, a visit of condolence. The leader makes you wear white, and leave your weapons at the threshold. The doors, when they open, are as tall as the sky and as quiet as a held breath.

choices.text: Bow at the threshold, deep and slow

effects.log: The doors accept it. A cold wind passes over you, not unfriendly, as if the house were sizing up a guest.

choices.text: Count the twelve doors above the lintel

effects.log: One is smaller and plainer than the others. You mark it, privately, and say nothing.

events.text: You enter by the pilgrim's postern, a small gate in the foot of the great wall, left unlocked so that someone, someday, might come to mourn. You wear no banner. The corridor beyond is long, empty, and polished to a mirror. In the mirror, a thousand years of faces pass, too fast, going the other way.

choices.text: Look down and keep walking

effects.log: It is a long walk. When you finally look up, the corridor has become a hall, and you are in it.

choices.text: Watch the faces go by

effects.log: They are the pantheon's worshippers, all of them, a procession with nowhere to go. You nod to each, and several nod back.

events.text: The safe road follows the Hall of Twelve, a colonnade where each pillar bears one law of a dead god. Rival delegations walk it side by side, reading the inscriptions with grave faces. One pillar reads: thou shalt not take what is not offered. Another: thou shalt not refuse what is. They seem to contradict. They do not.

choices.text: Read every law aloud, quietly

effects.log: Twelve, with one blank. Your voice drops at the blank without your meaning it.

choices.text: Choose the one law you will keep today

effects.log: You pick it. The pillar warms against your shoulder as you pass, and you feel strangely observed.

events.text: The beast road passes the Menagerie of Emblems, where the pantheon's sacred animals stand in stone and in memory: an owl, a ram, a serpent, a stag, a hare, each the size of a house. They are not alive. But the hare's ear twitches as you pass, and the owl's head turns very slightly to follow you.

choices.text: Bow to each animal in turn

effects.log: The stone stirs, then settles. It is the oldest courtesy of the old faith, and it works.

choices.text: Walk quickly, eyes on the floor

effects.log: The head of the owl turns the whole way round, and you feel it on the back of your neck for a mile.

events.text: The hidden road runs through a passage behind the thirteenth pillar, a pillar the dead pantheon never counted. You walk it blind, by touch, as you did in a life when you were their servant. At the end is a small room with a stool and a lamp, and on the stool a scrap of parchment on which is written one name, in a hand like your own.

choices.text: Read the name aloud

effects.log: The lamp flares. Somewhere in the house a throne creaks, as if turning to look. The name is a god's true name.

choices.text: Do not read it, and take the parchment folded

effects.log: Some names are not for saying. You keep it hidden, carried like a seed against the day it will be needed.

events.text: The twelve empty thrones turn, slowly, toward you, and the laws they hold fall quiet one by one. They have enforced themselves without a god to enforce them, and now a living guest has walked through all twelve and broken none. The twelfth throne, plain and unmarked, does something none of the others do: it offers a seat.

choices.text: Decline the seat, bowing

effects.log: The throne settles, content. Something is placed in your hand, gently: a god's true name, written small.

choices.text: Sit on the twelfth throne a moment

effects.log: It is cold and fits like a coat of someone else's. You rise, shaken, with a name behind your teeth.

events.text: The thrones judge you and find you wanting in one law, a small one, a law of manners. They do not punish. They simply decline to open the way until the debt is paid, and so you must stand in the empty hall for as long as it takes to understand what you owe. It takes a night. It is not the longest night of your life, but it is close.

choices.text: Pay the debt in words, aloud

effects.log: You apologise to the empty thrones for the thing you did. The thrones relax, and the door unlatches.

choices.text: Wait until the debt tires of you

effects.log: The hall lets you go in the end, as a house lets go of a patient guest. You are stiff, and wiser.

events.text: You slip past the thrones by never once turning your back on them, backing out step by deliberate step, in the manner of a courtier leaving a king. It is humiliating and very effective. The thrones, one by one, subside. The last law does not quite release you, but it does not forbid you either.

choices.text: Bow as you leave

effects.log: The twelve thrones incline, very slightly, in return. You do not stop walking backward until the door.

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the last throne

effects.log: It is empty. It is, you decide, the loneliest chair in any heaven. You carry the thought out with you.

events.text: {sr_sect} seals the god's true name in a lead casket and carries it in procession to the Ministry of Rites, where it will be held in trust, since a name once spoken cannot be unsaid. The delegation walks slowly, in white, in silence. People in the streets bow their heads, not knowing why.

choices.text: Walk at the back of the procession

effects.log: It is the best place to see the faces of the watchers. Some of them are weeping, and some are praying, and one is simply relieved.

choices.text: Carry the casket for one street

effects.log: It is lighter than you feared. By the end of the street you have felt a name settle against your ribs, as if testing the fit.

events.text: At the foot of the great stair a patrol of white-masked rite-wardens stands in a line, tall and thin, their long gloves folded across their chests. Their orders are to claim all relics from the Sealed Heaven. Their leader's voice is thin and flat, and he does not blink. The casket seems, suddenly, rather conspicuous.

choices.text: Unveil it and name the god aloud

effects.log: The wardens flinch. A name once spoken is held in the world. You have made it theirs to guard, and they bow, bewildered.

choices.text: Leave by the postern, in the white of a mourner

effects.log: You become the dullest face in the crowd. The wardens count heads and miss yours.

events.text: A smell of old smoke has crept into the upper heavens, thin and sweet, and a pale ash has begun to fall on the quiet terraces. The Ministry of Records identifies it at once: the Heaven Burned for Its Faith is turning back. Its people set fire to it themselves, rather than see it ruled by another god. The fire never went out.

choices.text: Ask a record-keeper what they believed

effects.log: She does not say. She takes a very small step back from the question. Then, quietly, she says: everything, all at once.

choices.text: Sweep the ash from your own threshold

effects.log: It comes back by dusk, finer than before. You sweep it again, and do not know why it matters.

events.text: {sr_sect} brings water-bearers in grey, each with a sealed gourd of cold river-water, for there is a rule that no one enters a burning house without leaving something behind to cool it. The Heaven rises ahead, a vast silhouette of char and ember. Faint bells ring in the heat. The leader says: not one drop to be used in anger.

choices.text: Carry your gourd without a word

effects.log: It is surprisingly heavy. The heat gathers on your face and does not trouble you; the water has been blessed.

choices.text: Pour a few drops on the threshold

effects.log: The embers hiss, as at a greeting. The gate, scorched and enormous, opens.

events.text: You enter by the water-gate, a channel where the burning city once drained its ashes. It is dry now, and warm. On the walls, in the half-light, you can see where hands have pressed against the stone, one after another, and left handprints in soot. You place your own on one. It fits perfectly.

choices.text: Leave your handprint beside theirs

effects.log: The soot is soft and cool. A warmth runs up your arm and settles under the shoulder.

choices.text: Keep your hands to yourself and hurry

effects.log: The handprints watch you pass. You feel more watched than hurried.

events.text: The safe road follows the Avenue of Cinders, a broad boulevard lined with charred statues of gods whose faces melted in the fire. Rival delegations walk it quickly, hands over mouths, eyes lowered. The heat is a pressure, not a pain. Overhead, the sky is the colour of old brass, and sparks fall slowly like snow.

choices.text: Stop and straighten a fallen statue

effects.log: It is heavy, and hot, and it takes three of you. When it stands, a pale breath leaves it. It was only waiting to be put upright.

choices.text: Pass quickly with your sleeve over your face

effects.log: The ash clings to you anyway. You are, by the gates, entirely grey.

events.text: The beast road passes the Salamander Courts, a series of red-lit cloisters where fire-lizards the size of dogs lounge in the heat. They are patient, indolent and watchful; they were temple pets, once, and have not forgotten their keepers' kindness. One climbs into your lap without being asked, glowing faintly, and begins to purr.

choices.text: Stroke it between the eyes

effects.log: It is warm as a hearthstone, and entirely contented. You carry the memory of it for a long time.

choices.text: Gently set it down and move on

effects.log: It sits in the dust, offended. But it follows you at a distance to the end of the courtyard.

events.text: The hidden road is a staircase of cooled lava that you once climbed barefoot, as a pilgrim, in a life you cannot quite recall. At the top is a small altar-fire, kept burning by no one, and beside it a bowl of the sweet ash. A folded cloth lies on the step, embroidered with your own faith-name in thread that has not scorched.

choices.text: Wear the cloth

effects.log: It settles on your shoulders like a hand. The fire on the altar leans toward you, in recognition.

choices.text: Add a pinch of the ash to the fire

effects.log: It flares white, once, and then burns blue. A small, sacred thing is done, and you carry it quietly out.

events.text: The last believer, a flame in the shape of a woman kneeling at a ruined altar, lifts her head. She has kept the faith for ten thousand years, in the dark, alone, and has never once doubted it. When she sees that you do not scorn her, her fire dims to the soft gold of a candle, and she holds out the god's last relic, wrapped in the cloth of her own sleeve.

choices.text: Receive it with both hands

effects.log: It is a little carved bowl, black with smoke. She bows to the ground. The Heaven exhales at last, and the ash settles.

choices.text: Kneel beside her a while

effects.log: You do not pray. You simply kneel. She seems to find this enough, and the fire in the ruin quiets by a shade.

events.text: The last believer's flame rises around you, not hot but certain, and holds you in a circle of her unwavering faith. For an hour you feel what it is to be wholly sure of something, and when she lets you go you are shaken to the roots of your own doubt. You walk out slowly, tender as a burn, and clean as a bell.

choices.text: Sit in the ash a while

effects.log: The doubts return, one at a time, like old neighbours. They are a comfort, in their way.

choices.text: Carry the certainty out with you

effects.log: It fades by the gates, as a warm coat does in the rain. But for a mile you were sure.

events.text: You slip past the last believer by kneeling as she kneels, a small shape among the ruins, one more silhouette at the altar. She glances sideways once, sees only a pilgrim, and looks away to her prayers. You rise very slowly and withdraw backward, with a feeling of enormous trespass and quiet gratitude.

choices.text: Leave a pinch of salt on the altar

effects.log: A very old courtesy to the burnt. The fire gives a single, tiny spark, and goes quiet.

choices.text: Walk out in complete silence

effects.log: The faint bells follow you to the gate and fall away. You find you are holding your breath for her.

events.text: {sr_sect} places the relic in the Hall of Remembrance, beneath a glass of clear water, and the delegation holds a vigil for a Heaven that chose its own ending. At dawn the leader proposes that the bowl be returned to the place where it was loved. Nobody argues. It is, you find, the first thing the delegation has agreed on all season.

choices.text: Volunteer to carry the bowl back

effects.log: You are told to wait for a year. A year later, the answer is yes, and you go.

choices.text: Add your name to the vigil list

effects.log: It is a long list. Your name is in the middle. It feels like belonging to a small, fierce, kind company.

events.text: At the burned gate a column of black-robed zealots from a rival pantheon waits in tidy ranks, torches unlit, hands raised in greeting. They claim the relic as the holy property of their faith, and they are, you note, genuinely moved. It is a worse position than villainy. They mean it.

choices.text: Show them the bowl, and let them touch it

effects.log: They weep, and bow, and one lays his forehead on the char. It was never theirs, but they will not forget the touch.

choices.text: Withdraw through the water-gate

effects.log: They do not see you go. They are lost in their prayers, which is the kindest way to leave a zealot.

events.text: Names have begun to go missing from the lesser temples. Not the gods themselves, only their names, quietly, off the lintels, out of the hymns, and from the tongues of the priests. The Ministry of Rites traces the thefts to the Ward of Unmaking, a sealed prison-heaven where the gods' enemies were kept. It is opening. Something in it is very hungry for what is called.

choices.text: Check that you still remember your own name

effects.log: You do. You say it aloud a few times, just to be sure. It sounds smaller than it did.

choices.text: Ask the priests what they have lost

effects.log: One cannot say. He knows only that there was a god here, once, and that something has been taken from the place where the god used to be.

events.text: {sr_sect} gives each member of the delegation a thread, tied round the wrist and knotted with a word you were told to pick yourself. The Ward's gate is plain iron, and cold. The leader says: remember your word. Do not say it aloud inside. Do not let anyone say it for you. The gate swings, with no sound at all.

choices.text: Choose the word of a person, not a god

effects.log: It is a small name, a plain one. You will need it, and in the cold it holds like a coal.

choices.text: Choose a word of your own invention

effects.log: It means nothing to anyone else. That may be its strength.

events.text: You slip in by the Ward's Warden-door, a narrow plug of iron that no warden has opened in a thousand years. Inside it is not dark but blank, a pale colourless emptiness in which only your breath and your heartbeat remain. You walk on a floor you cannot see, calling softly in your head the name you came in with.

choices.text: Hold your name in your teeth

effects.log: It is the oldest trick. It works. The blankness thins, grudgingly, and shows a ceiling, a wall.

choices.text: Count your breaths

effects.log: There is nothing else to count. By the thousandth the Ward gives up some of its pallor, in disgust.

events.text: The safe road follows the Cell Row, a long gallery of cells whose doors are open and whose prisoners are long gone. Rival delegations walk it in tight, uneasy groups. On every door is a chalked word: a name, struck through. You find a cell that bears the name of a god you once prayed to. It has been struck through twice.

choices.text: Wipe away one of the strike-throughs

effects.log: The chalk comes off under your thumb. The name, half-restored, glimmers faintly, and for the length of a breath you remember its hymn.

choices.text: Leave the cell as you found it

effects.log: There are things you cannot mend. You stand a moment in the door, and bow.

events.text: The beast road passes the Menagerie of the Forgotten, where beasts that had no name are chained in rows, pale and mute: unnamed things of all shapes, once worshipped, now only breathing. They watch you pass with the eyes of animals who have forgotten what they were for. A small grey one reaches through the bars, tentatively, to touch your sleeve.

choices.text: Give it a name, quietly

effects.log: You choose something plain and kind. The creature closes its eyes. A faint colour comes up through its fur.

choices.text: Gently loose its hand and go on

effects.log: It watches you go. You can feel the weight of its not-asking for a long, long way.

events.text: The hidden road is a vent behind the Warden's table, which you opened once, in a life you chose to forget. You crawl through, remembering. At the end is a cell, tidy as a monk's, with a single stool and a lamp that burns without oil. On the stool, a brass plate, engraved with a name that cannot be unmade. It is not yours. It is meant for you to carry.

choices.text: Pick up the plate

effects.log: It is heavier than the Ward, and warmer. Whatever name it bears, it will outlast anything that comes for it.

choices.text: Read the name and leave the plate

effects.log: You read it, once, and let it go. It will find its own way out, and you have the sense it knows you helped.

events.text: The god-eater, a vast hunger with no face, draws back from you as a tide draws from a rock that will not be moved. It has swallowed ten thousand names and never found one it could not digest. Yours it cannot even begin. It sets down, almost shyly, the one name it has never been able to unmake: the name that was given, not taken.

choices.text: Accept the name with both hands

effects.log: It is small, bright and impossible. The hunger shudders, and for a moment looks almost at peace.

choices.text: Tell the hunger its own name

effects.log: You say it softly. It is a name nobody has used in ages. The hunger sits, very still, and does not eat for a long time.

events.text: The god-eater takes your name, and nothing else. You do not feel it go. You feel only a sudden vast quiet, as if your life had become a room with the furniture gone. Then, from a pocket, your word, the one on the thread, comes back to you, whole. You remember who you are, and walk out holding it in both hands.

choices.text: Say your word aloud, softly, on the stair

effects.log: It returns to you completely. The hunger lets you go, without malice or regret.

choices.text: Sit and let the quiet settle

effects.log: It is peaceful, terribly. When you rise, you are more yourself than before, and a little afraid of it.

events.text: You slip past the god-eater by being, for a moment, nobody: you let go of your name entirely, and walk through the hunger as one walks through mist. It does not notice. When you pick the name up again on the far side, it is like putting on an old coat, slightly thinner at the elbows.

choices.text: Check your name twice

effects.log: It is all there. You are, for a moment, almost glad.

choices.text: Look back at the hunger

effects.log: It is eating something far off, a hymn, a title. You wish, briefly, that you could do something. You cannot.

events.text: {sr_sect} writes the name in gold on the plain wall of its principal temple, so that no one need carry it who does not wish to. Priests come to look. Some weep. Some pray. A few whisper the name aloud, once, and quickly stop. The wall is warm, and by evening there are flowers on the floor beneath.

choices.text: Leave a flower of your own

effects.log: It is a small thing. But the pile grows, and within the week it is a garden.

choices.text: Stand guard over the wall

effects.log: Someone must. You take the first watch, and are not relieved for a long while.

events.text: At the Ward's outer gate, three gaunt Archivists of the Ministry of Rites wait with a locked case and a printed warrant. They would like the name, for safekeeping. They would, one gathers, like to be the only keepers of any name that cannot be unmade. They speak of safety, and glance at the case, which has room for exactly one plate.

choices.text: Propose a shared keeping

effects.log: You write the terms yourself. They read them twice, and sign, with the grey look of people who have been outmanoeuvred by a kindness.

choices.text: Hide the plate among the temple bell-flags

effects.log: They search your satchel and find only prayers. Overhead, in the coloured flags, the name flutters, safe.

events.text: Beasts of every domain have begun to look at the sky and weep, without sorrow, as if hearing a very old, very kind voice. The oldest priests bar their doors. They know the sound. It means that the Spring Before Faith, the place where life first prayed to nothing and was answered, is breathing, and wants its children home.

choices.text: Listen from the roof of your temple

effects.log: It is a sound below sound, like a second heartbeat. Beasts gather at the foot of the steps, silent.

choices.text: Ask an old priest what it asks of gods

effects.log: He says: to remember that they were once guests. He says it very quietly, and does not look at the sky.

events.text: {sr_sect} walks its delegation to the Spring barefoot, with no banner, no tool and no name, as the old law demands. The leader says: before faith there was no priest. You walk down a green path, past trees that do not have names, and the sound of water grows from a murmur to a hush.

choices.text: Leave your shoes at the threshold

effects.log: The moss is cool and alive. You feel the world press softly against the soles of your feet, a welcome.

choices.text: Keep one thing, in your pocket

effects.log: Your amulet is warm. The Spring notices, and says nothing, and lets you pass.

events.text: You find the Spring's back door, a gap in the roots of a tree older than the heavens. It is damp and sweet-smelling, and the floor is carpeted in soft white fungus that glows. You crawl, and then crouch, and then stand, in a green cavern full of the sound of water, and of something breathing slowly in its sleep.

choices.text: Move softly along the wall

effects.log: The glow brightens as you pass, and dims behind. It is like being walked through by a lantern.

choices.text: Stop and listen to the breathing

effects.log: It matches yours, slowly. You are very calm. You are almost certain you are not alone.

events.text: The safe road follows the Pilgrim's Run, a worn way beside the stream where every faith's first priests walked, long before they had a faith. Rival delegations pass in a hush, heads bare. At each bend is a little cairn of river-stones, each placed by a different hand. You add one of your own.

choices.text: Add a stone to the cairn

effects.log: It is a small, warm gesture. A single bird sings, as if in approval.

choices.text: Count the stones in the cairns

effects.log: Nine thousand and some. You stop at the first thousand and listen to the water instead.

events.text: The beast road leads through the Meadow of First Things, where the earliest animals graze in the tall grass, not yet knowing what they are: half-deer, half-hare, a creature with the length of a snake and the patience of a stone. They look up as you pass and do not run. They have never seen anything to run from.

choices.text: Sit down among them

effects.log: They come, one at a time, to look at you. It is the oldest kind of kindness: not to be afraid.

choices.text: Walk through in single file with the delegation

effects.log: The meadow takes its time. When you are through, you feel strangely rested, and a little sorry.

events.text: The hidden road is a path along the roots of the first tree, which you recognise by a feeling in the soles of your feet, a homecoming. You walk it with your eyes closed. At the end, in a hollow of living wood, is a basin of clear water, so still it holds the sky. On its surface a single drop trembles, waiting for your hand.

choices.text: Touch the drop

effects.log: It runs up your finger like a thought. For a moment the world is simply good, and nothing needs to be named.

choices.text: Let the drop stay in its basin

effects.log: It trembles, and settles. The Spring approves. You leave with nothing, and the sense of having been trusted.

events.text: The first beast-god rises from the water, older than prayer, and vast. Its eyes are two quiet pools; its breath is the sound of rain on leaves. It does not fight. It looks at you for a long time, and in that look you see everything alive that ever walked into the dark and came back. It lowers its head and gives you, in the hollow of its nostril, a single drop of the first faith.

choices.text: Receive the drop, and bow

effects.log: It sits in your palm like a seed of light. The beast-god closes its eyes, as if it has been waiting for this its whole life.

choices.text: Ask what it would like

effects.log: It would like, it says, to be remembered by something that does not want anything from it. You tell it you will.

events.text: The first beast-god breathes out, once, and the breath rolls you over and over, soft as a wave, across the whole length of the Meadow. You come to rest in the grass beside a grazing half-deer, laughing, unharmed, and entirely beaten. The beast-god's great eyes close. The matter is, to it, concluded.

choices.text: Lie in the grass and look at the sky

effects.log: There is no sky here, only a lighter green. You watch it a long while.

choices.text: Thank the half-deer for the company

effects.log: It nibbles your sleeve, politely, and wanders off. The beast-god, from afar, hums.

events.text: You sit by the water and let your hands lie open on your knees, and say nothing at all. After a very long time, the first beast-god lays its enormous head beside you, close enough to feel the warmth of its breath. It does not want to be led, or served, or named. It wants to be sat with, as a creature that is not alone.

choices.text: Stay until the light moves

effects.log: It takes the whole afternoon. When you rise, the drop of faith is on your sleeve, bright as dew.

choices.text: Rest your hand on its brow

effects.log: The fur is warm and living, and the heartbeat beneath it is slow as a tide. It lets you, and it remembers.

events.text: {sr_sect} places the drop of first faith in a plain wooden bowl at the centre of its principal temple, uncovered, unlocked and unguarded, as the old custom requires. Within the week the bowl is the most-visited shrine in the domain. No priest says a word. The drop sits there, shining, and everyone who looks into it is quiet.

choices.text: Sit beside the bowl for an hour

effects.log: You do not pray. You do not ask for anything. It is, you realise, the first time you have not.

choices.text: Make a rota of those who wish to keep watch

effects.log: It is the right size for a temple to love. You keep the roll, and the bowl, humbly, for years.

events.text: On the road from the Spring a convoy of sleek black chariots has drawn up across the way. The banner of a sun-god flies from the first, and the god himself steps down, smiling, hand outstretched. He would like to hold the drop, he says, for just a moment, to bless it. His retinue is large, and has a way of standing without sitting.

choices.text: Let him look, but not touch

effects.log: He looks long, and wistfully. Something in his face softens. He bows, and lets the road be.

choices.text: Cross the stream where the chariots cannot

effects.log: Water holds the wheels. By the time they have turned, you are in the trees, with a drop in your hand and a laugh in your throat.

events.text: Music has begun to drift down from the upper heavens at odd hours, a cheerful, tireless music, and half the minor gods are humming it without knowing. The Ministry of Rites knows better. The Festival That Never Ended is opening again, a feast whose god died mid-toast, and whose guests have been celebrating for ten thousand years because no one has dared to say the night is over.

choices.text: Ask a revellers' envoy what they are celebrating

effects.log: He cannot remember. He says that is the beauty of it. His smile does not reach his eyes, and his glass is empty.

choices.text: Hum along, to see what it does

effects.log: You catch yourself tapping a foot. A friend takes your arm. The tune will stay with you for a week.

events.text: {sr_sect} dresses the delegation in festival masks of paper and gilt, as the invitation required. The leader assigns each of you a task: watch the host, watch the door, watch each other. The gate is garlanded with flowers that never wilt. Beyond it, the music swells, and a thousand glasses chime.

choices.text: Wear the mask with good humour

effects.log: It is lighter than it looks. By the second courtyard you have forgotten you are wearing it, which is the danger.

choices.text: Keep one eye on the door

effects.log: There is one, behind the third pillar, unmarked. You track it carefully through all the feasting.

events.text: You enter as a servant, through the kitchen yard where the festival's endless supply of sweet cakes is kept coming. A cook, red-faced and cheerful, hands you a tray without a word. It is heavy. It smells of honey, saffron and something sad. You walk in among the guests, among the glitter, unremarked.

choices.text: Serve a few tables with a straight face

effects.log: Nobody looks at you. A servant is invisible. You learn a great deal about the feast in an hour.

choices.text: Set the tray down and slip away

effects.log: The cook looks after you with perfect comprehension. You nod. He nods. It is a conspiracy of two.

events.text: The safe road follows the Grand Promenade, a wide avenue lined with feast-tables and dancing couples. Rival delegations press through it in masks, laughing too loudly, determined to look as though they are enjoying themselves. A woman in a crown of paper stars catches your sleeve and says she has been dancing for four hundred years. Would you like to cut in?

choices.text: Dance one dance with her

effects.log: She is warm and tired and grateful. When the tune ends, she holds your hands a moment longer than the step requires.

choices.text: Decline and press on

effects.log: She nods, unsurprised, and finds another partner within the minute. The feast moves on, as ever.

events.text: The beast road passes through the Menagerie of Delights, where festival-animals are kept for the amusement of the guests: a dancing bear in a waistcoat, a peacock with a gold clasp, a tiny elephant who juggles lanterns. They are gentle, and they are tired. The bear catches your eye and, very discreetly, puts a paw to his lips.

choices.text: Open the pen quietly

effects.log: They walk out, one by one, into the dusk, and no one notices. The elephant takes a lantern with him as a keepsake.

choices.text: Applaud, and move on

effects.log: They bow to you, politely, as they have bowed to everyone. You feel the small, miserable weight of having done nothing.

events.text: The hidden road is a service stair behind the high table, which you swept in a life when you were a servant here. At the top, in a little room above the feast, a table is laid for one. The cup is half full of tea gone cold. A card beside it reads, in your hand: you may leave, if you want to. Beneath it lies a sealed pouch of ten thousand years of unspent joy.

choices.text: Take the pouch

effects.log: It is light and tingling in the palm. You feel years of laughter in the cloth, undiminished, patient.

choices.text: Finish the cold tea, and rise

effects.log: It tastes of the best evening you ever had. When you set it down, the toast is complete.

events.text: The masked host, the keeper of the festival, who has never been permitted to let a guest leave, stops mid-bow. It sees you are unmoved by the music and unmasked by the dance, and in that moment realises it has been waiting a long time for someone who would say the night was over. It takes the pouch of unspent joy from its sleeve and presses it into your hand.

choices.text: Say the night is over, and thank it

effects.log: The mask of the host cracks across the brow, and under it is a face that has been smiling too long. It weeps, with relief. The music stops.

choices.text: Take the pouch and ask the host to rest

effects.log: It does. It sits on the nearest bench like someone who has forgotten how, and falls asleep at once.

events.text: The host catches your hand and will not release it. It leads you, courteous as a prince, into a dance that goes on for an hour, and then another, and then, you think, a night. When at last the music pauses and the host steps back to bow, you are dizzy, delighted and quite unable to remember why you came. The door is open. You are still smiling.

choices.text: Find the door by the glow of the street lamps

effects.log: It is there, as promised. The cold air outside is a slap, and a blessing.

choices.text: Ask for one more dance

effects.log: The host is delighted. You leave at dawn, and sleep for two days, and do not regret it.

events.text: You slip past the host by joining the dance and spinning, twirl by twirl, through the crowd to the far door, a step ahead of its gaze. It is a bold gambit in a crowded hall, and the music helps. At the threshold you take off your mask and set it on the cold stone, and a thousand voices behind you lift in a song you almost know.

choices.text: Leave the mask for the next guest

effects.log: It lies there, bright and gilt in the dark. You did not take anything you did not bring.

choices.text: Keep the mask as a souvenir

effects.log: It hums when you hold it. You will wonder, for a long time, whether it is lonely.

events.text: {sr_sect} brings the pouch of unspent joy to the High Temple and spends it, a pinch at a time, on the poor of the lower domains: a day of laughter for a widow, a night of ease for a dying man, a warm morning for a lonely child. It is the first time anyone in the delegation has spent anything without counting. The leader stops counting at noon.

choices.text: Carry the pouch to the widow

effects.log: She laughs for an hour, helplessly, and then cries, and then laughs again. She does not ask where it came from.

choices.text: Watch from the gate, and keep the count

effects.log: Someone must. You write down every name, and at the end of the day the list is the only gift the delegation can keep.

events.text: On the outer stair a thin company of costumed revellers has decided that the festival is not yet over. They block the way, singing, with glasses held aloft, arms linked, a wall of smiles. Their toast is for the guest of honour, and you are the guest. Several of them are weeping. All of them are sincere. None of them will let you pass.

choices.text: Drink one toast with them, and say it is the last

effects.log: It takes some courage. The revellers fall quiet, then cheer, and then, one by one, set down their glasses and go home.

choices.text: Slip away in the confusion of the toast

effects.log: A hundred glasses clink at once. In the sound, you walk down the stair as just another guest, leaving.

events.text: The delegations gather at the seal of {sr_realm} in their colours, incense rising, and names are read from a tablet of white jade. {sr_sect} has chosen its entrants. Yours is not among them. You watch the chosen walk through the seal, and it closes behind them like a lid over a bowl of water.

choices.text: Look along the seal for a flaw

effects.log: Seals are drawn by hands, and hands tire. You walk its rim slowly, noting where the line wavers.

choices.text: Go back to the shrine and keep vigil

effects.log: Next time they will read your name. You promise it, to no one in particular, in front of the altar.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: It goes down hard and stays down. You breathe the incense until it settles.

events.text: No delegation takes you in. You stand at the edge of the seal beneath the temple lamps while the pantheons file past toward {sr_realm}, and nobody so much as looks your way. A water-seller, packing up her cart, asks if you are lost. You laugh a little, and say no.

choices.text: Buy her last cup and sit on the steps

effects.log: It is cold temple water with a leaf in it. She tells you a story about her sister in the heavens, and you listen to all of it.

choices.text: Walk the seal alone

effects.log: There is a thin place to the north where the glyphs are cracked. You mark it for later.

events.text: A great realm is opening and the tablets are stern. Only the highest of every pantheon are read out, and the rest stand about in festival robes. A young acolyte behind you whispers that the choosing was fair. You know that it was, which is the worst part. The seal brightens, and the chosen go in.

choices.text: Bless the chosen aloud

effects.log: Several turn and bow. It costs nothing, and it lands somewhere.
